sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: One reference example. Use it only if you get stuck.

items.prompt: A has expected payoff $12, B has $9. Which, and what is ignored?

steps: A has the higher expected value.
Spread and risk tolerance are not captured.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: Assess whether this is a fair decision mechanism: choosing between two people using a single fair coin flip.
choices: Fair, because any random device produces a fair decision.
Fair; each person has probability 1/2, and the mechanism gives neither an advantage.
Not fair; the three probabilities are 3/6, 2/6, and 1/6, which are unequal.
Fair; each person receives probability 2/6 = 1/3, so the assignment is equal.

items.prompt: A game costs $7 to play. It pays $72 with probability 1/4 and nothing otherwise. Find the expected value to the player, and say whether the game is fair.
choices: $18; the game is favourable to the player
$11; the game is favourable to the player
$65; the game is favourable to the player
$-7; the game is unfavourable to the player

items.prompt: An insurer charges a premium of $17 and pays out $275 with probability 1/55. Find the insurer's expected profit per policy.
Option A has expected payoff $17 and Option B has expected payoff $15. On expected value alone, which should be chosen, and what does this criterion ignore?
choices: Neither; expected value cannot compare two options.
Option B; expected value ignores the spread of outcomes and the decider's tolerance for risk.
Option A; expected value already accounts for risk, so nothing is ignored.
Option A; expected value ignores the spread of outcomes and the decider's tolerance for risk.

items.prompt: Assess whether this is a fair decision mechanism: choosing between three people by rolling a standard die, assigning two faces to each.
choices: Not fair; the three probabilities are 3/6, 2/6, and 1/6, which are unequal.
Fair; each person has probability 1/2, and the mechanism gives neither an advantage.
Fair, because any random device produces a fair decision.
Fair; each person receives probability 2/6 = 1/3, so the assignment is equal.
